paras: The lynching of John J. Moore took place on June 17, 1879, when an armed band took Moore, a white man, from the custody of the Spartanburg County, South Carolina, sheriff and hanged him near the spot where a young white woman's body had been found. Moore had been jailed on suspicion of the rape and murder of Frances Woodward, and he denied his guilt before a crowd of about 600. Papers outside the state noted that the man lynched was white, and a Spartanburg grand jury later declined to condemn the lynchers.

On Sunday, June 8, two men passing a road near Duncan's Station, on the Air Line railroad, found the body of a young white woman in the woods, shot in the breast and with her throat cut. She had come from Pickens County looking for an uncle, ate dinner at Moore's house and was last seen leaving with him. A coroner's jury returned a verdict of death 'by person unknown', but Moore was arrested and jailed at Spartanburg, and the Abbeville Press and Banner reported that feeling was so high he would probably be lynched.

The News and Courier's Spartanburg correspondent described Moore as a farmer, storekeeper and distiller with a 'very bad' reputation and cited tracks matching his shoes and blood on his trousers. According to a second Anderson Intelligencer account, about a hundred men meeting at Dantzler's Bridge on June 14 held a 'Judge Lynch' trial and found Moore 'guilty'.

Around midnight on Monday, June 16, between 150 and 200 armed men rode into Spartanburg, posted pickets on the roads and searched the jail. Sheriff Thompson, warned in advance, had hidden Moore under a bridge beside the Air Line railroad with a few guards, meaning to put him on an engine for Columbia. One squad found him, overpowered the guards and carried him by buggy to the woods where the body had been found, twelve or seventeen miles away.

By morning a crowd of about 500 or 600 had gathered, and the News and Courier correspondent reported that 'all classes and ages' took part and no one wore a disguise. Some urged burning or torture, but a 'committee of arrangements' refused. Maj. J. W. Woodward of Winnsboro urged the crowd to wait for the law and was ignored. Two men drew a buggy from under Moore, roped to a post oak limb; he was pronounced dead after thirty-nine minutes.

Judge Pressley put the lynching before the Spartanburg grand jury, warning that 'no man would be safe' if such violence went on. The jury replied that citizens had lynched Moore but had 'merely anticipated the sentence of the law of the land', and no indictment was reported. In November a monument paid for by subscription was raised to Frances Woodward at Middle Tyger Church, with an inscription saying she 'Died defending her virtue, June 5, 1879.'

Charleston and Augusta dispatches ran on June 17 and 18 in Richmond, Memphis, Cincinnati and New York, where the Tribune headed it 'The Hasty Lynching of a White Man.' The Charleston dispatch stressed that 'Moore and his victim were both white.' South Carolina papers dwelt on the crowd's order; the Anderson Intelligencer headed its account 'Vengeance, Swift and Sure!' and wrote that 'the entire community was in hearty sympathy' with the lynching.

Elsewhere the case drew political comment. The Republican National Republican answered Democratic claims that this was the state's first lynching in years by saying that 'Hundreds, if not thousands' of attacks on Black Republican voters had gone uncounted. The Arizona Silver Belt called the grand jury's presentment 'most extraordinary' for 'justifying the act.' Two years later the Pickens Sentinel named Moore, 'a white man in Spartanburg county', as the first man lynched in the state for rape, in an editorial disputing the Abbeville Press and Banner's charge that the state habitually lynched Black people.

The hour of the hanging is given as 7, 8 or 10 o'clock, and the woman as Frances Woodward, Mary Woodward or Francis Heaton, names the Spartanburg dispatch explained by her mother's two marriages. The Shenandoah Herald, summarizing The Sun, said Moore 'made confession', but the Augusta dispatch and both detailed South Carolina accounts say he insisted he was innocent. One report says his sister, another his wife, was offered a choice of burning or hanging, while the News and Courier correspondent wrote that the committee refused to allow burning.

Separate Charleston, Augusta and Spartanburg dispatches and two detailed South Carolina accounts agree on the seizure and hanging (A4, A6, A11, A12).

accounts.label: Wire reports (Charleston, Augusta)
accounts.gist: 150 armed horsemen came to the jail; the sheriff had moved Moore, but the lynchers seized him and hanged him near the murder scene; the Augusta dispatch says he asserted his innocence.

accounts.label: News and Courier special correspondent
accounts.gist: An eyewitness account of an orderly, organized crowd of 600 that refused proposals to burn Moore and hanged him at 7 a.m. while he denied his guilt.

accounts.label: Second Anderson Intelligencer account
accounts.gist: Recounts inquest evidence, a lynch 'trial' at Dantzler's Bridge, the capture of Moore under a log bridge and his hanging before about 600; says the entire community approved.

accounts.label: Shenandoah Herald after The Sun
accounts.gist: Hanged in daylight before about 500 after invitations went to the neighbors; says he 'made confession' and that his sister was offered the choice of burning or hanging.

accounts.label: Spartanburg grand jury
accounts.gist: Found that citizens lynched Moore in obedience to justice, anticipating the law's sentence.

framing.detail: The Anderson Intelligencer ran the account under 'Vengeance, Swift and Sure!', called Moore 'the Wretch', and stressed the crowd's quiet order and the community's 'hearty sympathy'.
Northern papers carried short wire items, the New-York Tribune headed 'The Hasty Lynching of a White Man' and noting he asserted his innocence.
The Republican National Republican used the case to charge that lynching of Black Republican voters went uncounted.
The Arizona Silver Belt criticized the grand jury for 'justifying the act'.
In 1881 the Pickens Sentinel called Moore 'the first fiend who met the vengeance of an outraged community for rape' to rebut a charge that the state habitually lynched Black people.

conflicts.note: The body was found on Sunday the 8th (A2, A12), so the 9th cannot be the date of death; the monument inscription (A16) gives June 5.
The Spartanburg dispatch says she was known by both surnames because her mother had married twice (A11); the monument reads Frances Woodward (A16).
Ten o'clock was the announced hour (A4, A11); the eyewitness dispatch says the crowd grew impatient and hanged him at 7.

conflicts.note: The two detailed South Carolina accounts and the Augusta dispatch all report denials; the Shenandoah Herald's claim is a secondhand summary.

info: Moore was seized on the night of Monday, June 16, 1879, and hanged on the morning of Tuesday, June 17, 1879; the reported hour varies (7, 8 or 10 a.m.).

Hanged from a post oak in the woods near where the woman's body had been found, near Duncan's Station / Duncan's Cross Roads, described as near Welford and near Vernonsville; reported as 12 or 17 miles from Spartanburg.
John J. Moore, a white farmer, storekeeper and licensed distiller, aged 40 to 45, with a wife and five children.
Accused of the 'outrage' (rape) and murder of a young white woman, Frances Woodward (also called Francis Heaton, or Mary Woodward), from Pickens County.
An armed mounted band that rode into Spartanburg, organized in squads under leaders and a 'committee of arrangements'; no disguises were worn and 'all classes and ages' reportedly took part.
